expectedText:
PREMARITAL AGREEMENT
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND INTENT TO MARRY
This Premarital Agreement is entered into by Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee ("the parties"), who state that they intend to marry each other and that this Agreement is made in contemplation of that marriage. The parties anticipate marrying on or about June 14, 2027. This Agreement sets out the parties' understanding regarding property and support matters as described in the sections that follow.

WHAT A PREMARITAL AGREEMENT IS, AND WHEN IT TAKES EFFECT
California statute defines a "premarital agreement" as an agreement between prospective spouses made in contemplation of marriage and to be effective upon marriage. This document is intended by Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee to be such an agreement. Under the same statutory scheme, a premarital agreement becomes effective upon marriage — it has no effect if the parties do not marry.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "“Premarital agreement” means an agreement between prospective spouses made in contemplation of marriage and to be effective upon marriage."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1610(a) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory definition of a premarital agreement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1610.)
  "A premarital agreement becomes effective upon marriage."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1613 (California Legislative Information text), when a premarital agreement becomes effective (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1613.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a premarital agreement is defined and triggered — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement. Family law, including whether and how prospective spouses may contract before marriage, varies by state; a document intended for use in another state is evidence of nothing beyond what that state's own law provides.

EXECUTION REQUIREMENTS
Under this statute, a premarital agreement must be in writing and signed by both prospective spouses. This document is intended to be signed by Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee before the marriage occurring on or planned for June 14, 2027.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A premarital agreement shall be in writing and signed by both parties."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1611 (California Legislative Information text), the written-and-signed execution requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1611.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the minimum written-and-signed formality some states impose on premarital agreements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement, and not a claim that no other formality (such as notarization, witnesses, or particular disclosure procedures) is ever required by a court applying a different rule or a different provision of the same body of law. This is a single statutory section (§ 1611); no additional independent source was found for this.

NO CONSIDERATION REQUIRED
Under this statute, a premarital agreement — and any later written amendment or revocation of one signed after marriage — is enforceable without consideration, meaning without either party having to show they received something of value in exchange for signing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "It is enforceable without consideration."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1611 (California Legislative Information text), no consideration required for the original agreement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1611.)
  "The amended agreement or the revocation is enforceable without consideration."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1614 (California Legislative Information text), no consideration required for a post-marital amendment or revocation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1614.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that at least one state does not require consideration to enforce a premarital agreement or a post-marital amendment of one — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement, and not a claim that every state dispenses with consideration the same way.

WHAT A PREMARITAL AGREEMENT CAN ADDRESS
Under this statute, prospective spouses may contract with respect to: (1) the rights and obligations of each party in property either or both of them acquire, wherever located; (2) the right to buy, sell, use, transfer, exchange, abandon, lease, consume, expend, assign, encumber, mortgage, dispose of, or otherwise manage and control property; (3) the disposition of property on separation, marital dissolution, death, or another specified event; (4) the making of a will, trust, or other arrangement to carry out the agreement; (5) ownership and disposition of life insurance death benefits; (6) the choice of law governing the agreement's construction; and (7) any other matter, including personal rights and obligations, not in violation of public policy or a criminal statute. Two further, separately-sourced statutory limits on this list — concerning child support and spousal support — are addressed elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Parties to a premarital agreement may contract with respect to all of the following: (1) The rights and obligations of each of the parties in any of the property of either or both of them whenever and wherever acquired or located. (2) The right to buy, sell, use, transfer, exchange, abandon, lease, consume, expend, assign, create a security interest in, mortgage, encumber, dispose of, or otherwise manage and control property. (3) The disposition of property upon separation, marital dissolution, death, or the occurrence or nonoccurrence of any other event. (4) The making of a will, trust, or other arrangement to carry out the provisions of the agreement. (5) The ownership rights in and disposition of the death benefit from a life insurance policy. (6) The choice of law governing the construction of the agreement. (7) Any other matter, including their personal rights and obligations, not in violation of public policy or a statute imposing a criminal penalty."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1612(a) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory list of permitted subject matter (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1612.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's list of permitted subject matter for a premarital agreement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement, and not a claim that another state's list is identical. This is a single statutory section (§ 1612); no additional independent source was found for this.

CHILD SUPPORT CANNOT BE LIMITED BY THIS AGREEMENT
Under this statute, the right of a child to support may not be adversely affected by a premarital agreement between Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, regardless of what property or support terms the agreement otherwise contains.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The right of a child to support may not be adversely affected by a premarital agreement."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1612(b) (California Legislative Information text), child support is not adversely affected by the agreement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1612.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that at least one state places child support outside what a premarital agreement can alter — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement. Child support is typically treated by courts as belonging to the child rather than the parents, and statutory protection of it from private agreement is common, but its exact scope and mechanics vary by state. This is a single statutory section (§ 1612); no additional independent source was found for this.

SPOUSAL SUPPORT WAIVERS — THE INDEPENDENT-COUNSEL AND UNCONSCIONABILITY CONDITIONS
Under this statute, a provision in a premarital agreement addressing spousal support — including a waiver of it — is not enforceable if the party against whom it is being enforced was not represented by independent counsel at the time the agreement containing the provision was signed, or if the provision is unconscionable at the time enforcement is sought. The same statute states that an otherwise-unenforceable spousal support provision does not become enforceable merely because the party against whom enforcement is sought had independent counsel — independent representation is a condition for enforceability, not a guarantee of it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Any provision in a premarital agreement regarding spousal support, including, but not limited to, a waiver of it, is not enforceable if the party against whom enforcement of the spousal support provision is sought was not represented by independent counsel at the time the agreement containing the provision was signed, or if the provision regarding spousal support is unconscionable at the time of enforcement. An otherwise unenforceable provision in a premarital agreement regarding spousal support may not become enforceable solely because the party against whom enforcement is sought was represented by independent counsel."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1612(c) (California Legislative Information text), the independent-counsel and unconscionability conditions on spousal-support provisions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1612.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's specific double condition on spousal-support provisions in a premarital agreement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement. Some states do not permit prospective spouses to limit spousal support at all; others impose different conditions. This is a single statutory section (§ 1612); no additional independent source was found for this.

FINANCIAL DISCLOSURE AND PROPERTY SCHEDULE REFERENCE
Each party has attached to this Agreement, as Schedule A (Jordan Alex Lee) and Schedule B (Morgan Casey Lee), a listing of that party's property, assets, and financial obligations as of the date below. The parties acknowledge that these schedules are incorporated into this Agreement by reference. ☐ Schedule A and Schedule B attached.

WHEN A PREMARITAL AGREEMENT IS NOT ENFORCEABLE
Under this statute, a premarital agreement is not enforceable if the party against whom enforcement is sought proves either that the party did not execute the agreement voluntarily, or that the agreement was unconscionable when executed and, before execution, the party was not provided a fair, reasonable, and full disclosure of the other party's property or financial obligations; did not voluntarily and expressly waive, in writing, the right to disclosure beyond what was provided; and did not have, and could not reasonably have had, adequate knowledge of the other party's property or financial obligations. The same statute directs that whether an agreement is unconscionable is decided by the court as a matter of law, not a question of fact for a jury.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A premarital agreement is not enforceable if the party against whom enforcement is sought proves either of the following: (1) That party did not execute the agreement voluntarily. (2) The agreement was unconscionable when it was executed and, before execution of the agreement, all of the following applied to that party: (A) That party was not provided a fair, reasonable, and full disclosure of the property or financial obligations of the other party. (B) That party did not voluntarily and expressly waive, in writing, any right to disclosure of the property or financial obligations of the other party beyond the disclosure provided. (C) That party did not have, or reasonably could not have had, an adequate knowledge of the property or financial obligations of the other party. (b) An issue of unconscionability of a premarital agreement shall be decided by the court as a matter of law."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1615(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), the two-part unenforceability test (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1615.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's two-part test for unenforceability — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement. Standards for involuntariness, unconscionability, and required financial disclosure between prospective spouses vary by state. This is a single statutory section (§ 1615); no additional independent source was found for this.

THE VOLUNTARINESS PRESUMPTION — INDEPENDENT COUNSEL AND THE SEVEN-DAY RULE
Under this statute, for purposes of the voluntariness test, a premarital agreement is deemed not executed voluntarily unless a court finds, in writing or on the record, that the party against whom enforcement is sought was represented by independent legal counsel at the time of signing, or, after being advised to seek independent counsel, expressly waived that representation in a separate writing — with the advisement to seek counsel required at least seven calendar days before the final agreement was signed. For an agreement executed between January 1, 2002 and January 1, 2020, the statute further requires that the party against whom enforcement is sought had not less than seven calendar days between first being presented with the final agreement and advised to seek independent counsel, and the time the agreement was signed. For an agreement executed on or after January 1, 2020, the statute instead requires not less than seven calendar days between first being presented with the final agreement and the time it was signed, regardless of whether that party was represented by counsel. Neither seven-day requirement applies to nonsubstantive amendments that do not change the agreement's terms. If the party against whom enforcement is sought was unrepresented by counsel, the statute additionally requires that the party was fully informed, in writing memorialized before signing, of the agreement's terms and basic effect and of the rights and obligations being given up, in a language the party was proficient in, and that the unrepresented party executed, on or before signing, a document declaring receipt of that information and identifying who provided it. The statute also requires a finding that the agreement and related writings were not executed under duress, fraud, or undue influence, that the parties had capacity to enter into the agreement, and permits the court to weigh any other relevant factors.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "For the purposes of subdivision (a), it shall be deemed that a premarital agreement was not executed voluntarily unless the court finds in writing or on the record all of the following: (1) The party against whom enforcement is sought was represented by independent legal counsel at the time of signing the agreement or, after being advised to seek independent legal counsel, expressly waived, in a separate writing, representation by independent legal counsel. The advisement to seek independent legal counsel shall be made at least seven calendar days before the final agreement is signed. (2) One of the following: (A) For an agreement executed between January 1, 2002, and January 1, 2020, the party against whom enforcement is sought had not less than seven calendar days between the time that party was first presented with the final agreement and advised to seek independent legal counsel and the time the agreement was signed. This requirement does not apply to nonsubstantive amendments that do not change the terms of the agreement. (B) For an agreement executed on or after January 1, 2020, the party against whom enforcement is sought had not less than seven calendar days between the time that party was first presented with the final agreement and the time the agreement was signed, regardless of whether the party is represented by legal counsel. This requirement does not apply to nonsubstantive amendments that do not change the terms of the agreement. (3) The party against whom enforcement is sought, if unrepresented by legal counsel, was fully informed of the terms and basic effect of the agreement as well as the rights and obligations the party was giving up by signing the agreement, and was proficient in the language in which the explanation of the party's rights was conducted and in which the agreement was written. The explanation of the rights and obligations relinquished shall be memorialized in writing and delivered to the party prior to signing the agreement. The unrepresented party shall, on or before the signing of the premarital agreement, execute a document declaring that the party received the information required by this paragraph and indicating who provided that information. (4) The agreement and the writings executed pursuant to paragraphs (1) and (3) were not executed under duress, fraud, or undue influence, and the parties did not lack capacity to enter into the agreement. (5) Any other factors the court deems relevant."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1615(c) (California Legislative Information text), the voluntariness presumption and its conditions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1615.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's specific voluntariness presumption, its seven-calendar-day mechanic, and its independent-counsel and unrepresented-party conditions — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement, and not a claim that seven days (or any waiting period, counsel requirement, or disclosure procedure) is required in any other state. This is a single statutory section (§ 1615); no additional independent source was found for this.

AMENDMENT AND REVOCATION AFTER MARRIAGE
Under this statute, after marriage a premarital agreement between Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee may be amended or revoked only by a written agreement signed by both parties.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "After marriage, a premarital agreement may be amended or revoked only by a written agreement signed by the parties."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1614 (California Legislative Information text), the written-agreement requirement for amendment or revocation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1614.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that at least one state requires a signed writing from both spouses to amend or revoke a premarital agreement after marriage — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement or amendment. This is a single statutory section (§ 1614); no additional independent source was found for this.

STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS — TOLLED DURING MARRIAGE, SUBJECT TO LACHES
Under this statute, any statute of limitations that would otherwise apply to a claim for relief under a premarital agreement is tolled — paused — during the marriage of the parties to the agreement. The same statute preserves equitable defenses limiting the time for enforcement, including laches and estoppel, as available to either party.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Any statute of limitations applicable to an action asserting a claim for relief under a premarital agreement is tolled during the marriage of the parties to the agreement. However, equitable defenses limiting the time for enforcement, including laches and estoppel, are available to either party."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1617 (California Legislative Information text), tolling during marriage, and preserved equitable defenses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1617.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's tolling rule for claims arising under a premarital agreement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement, and not a claim that every state tolls limitations periods during marriage the same way. This is a single statutory section (§ 1617); no additional independent source was found for this.

IF THE MARRIAGE IS LATER DETERMINED VOID
Under this statute, if a marriage is later determined to be void, an agreement that would otherwise have been a premarital agreement between Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee is enforceable only to the extent necessary to avoid an inequitable result.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "If a marriage is determined to be void, an agreement that would otherwise have been a premarital agreement is enforceable only to the extent necessary to avoid an inequitable result."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1616 (California Legislative Information text), enforceability limited to avoiding an inequitable result if the marriage is void (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1616.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how at least one state treats a premarital agreement when the underlying marriage is later found void — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement or a specific marriage's validity. This is a single statutory section (§ 1616); no additional independent source was found for this.

SIGNATURES AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the parties have signed this Agreement on the date(s) indicated below.

Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

Morgan Casey Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

Notary acknowledgment block, if used, follows on a separate page.

(B) For an agreement executed on or after January 1, 2020, the party against whom enforcement is sought had not less than seven calendar days between the time that party was first presented with the final agreement and the time the agreement was signed, regardless of whether the party is represented by legal counsel. This requirement does not apply to nonsubstantive amendments that do not change the terms of the agreement. (3) The party against whom enforcement is sought, if unrepresented by legal counsel, was fully informed of the terms and basic effect of the agreement as well as the rights and obligations the party was giving up by signing the agreement, and was proficient in the language in which the explanation of the party's rights was conducted and in which the agreement was written. The explanation of the rights and obligations relinquished shall be memorialized in writing and delivered to the party prior to signing the agreement. The unrepresented party shall, on or before the signing of the premarital agreement, execute a document declaring that the party received the information required by this paragraph and indicating who provided that information. (4) The agreement and the writings executed pursuant to paragraphs (1) and (3) were not executed under duress, fraud, or undue influence, and the parties did not lack capacity to enter into the agreement. (5) Any other factors the court deems relevant.
